content: Recent updates have been made to the algorithm for monitoring HIV treatment. The first viral load (VL) test should be conducted and reviewed by the six-month follow-up visit after initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). Subsequent VL monitoring should continue at 12 months post-ART initiation and annually thereafter. If a second VL test is required after adherence counseling, enhanced adherence support should be provided between tests. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines aim to differentiate between treatment failure (VL > 1000 copies/mL) and undetectable thresholds. Individuals with detectable but suppressed VL should be closely monitored, similar to those with VL > 1000 copies/mL, but treatment changes should be carefully considered, especially for those on dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens. Monitoring viral suppression and undetectable VL levels is essential for the health and well-being of people living with HIV and for evaluating the quality of treatment programs. All VL tests require follow-up actions. Patients with undetectable VL may be considered for differentiated service delivery (DSD) programs or commended for maintaining their target VL. Those with detectable viremia should receive follow-up care, including enhanced adherence counseling, repeat VL testing, and potential treatment changes if necessary. Increasing the proportion of individuals with undetectable VL can significantly improve patient health, reduce transmission, and decrease morbidity and mortality. Retention in ART programs is critical for achieving viral suppression and reducing mortality. Long-term retention remains a challenge, impacting patient health, the emergence of drug resistance, and onward HIV transmission. Silent transfers, where patients move between facilities without formal documentation, contribute to attrition rates. Improved patient monitoring systems using unique identifiers (UIDs) can facilitate information sharing and tracking across facilities, enhancing retention and care outcomes. Routine analysis of ART attrition data at facility and subnational levels can identify gaps in care and inform program improvements. Loss to follow-up (LTFU) refers to individuals who do not return for HIV care or medication refills. Many LTFU cases are due to undocumented transfers, deaths, or treatment discontinuation. Strengthening data flow between facilities and community services is essential for re-engaging patients in care and accurately measuring outcomes. The definition of LTFU has been revised from 90 days to 28 days since the last missed appointment to improve timely identification and re-engagement. Patient monitoring tools, such as the HIV card and ART register, are primary data sources for tracking retention and LTFU. Treatment interruptions can lead to viral rebound, immune decompensation, and clinical progression. Individuals may stop ART for various reasons, often without notifying healthcare providers. The concept of a revolving door of HIV care recognizes the cyclical nature of engagement and re-engagement in care. Addressing treatment interruptions requires timely interventions and monitoring to prevent life-threatening complications. Advanced HIV disease (AHD) is defined by a CD4 count <200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease. All children under five years of age living with HIV are considered to have AHD. These individuals are at higher risk of mortality and require close monitoring during ART initiation to detect immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) and other adverse events. Rapid tracing and follow-up of individuals with AHD or missed appointments are critical to reducing mortality. Common causes of death include tuberculosis (TB), cryptococcal disease, severe bacterial infections, and invasive fungal infections. WHO recommends a package of care for AHD, including diagnostic tests, prophylaxis, treatment, and tailored adherence counseling. Monitoring antiretroviral (ARV) drug toxicity is increasingly important as ART programs scale up and transition to newer ARVs with improved safety profiles. ARV-associated toxicities remain a common reason for non-adherence, treatment discontinuation, or drug substitution. WHO recommends a combination of approaches to monitor ARV toxicity, including active and routine surveillance, particularly in vulnerable populations such as pregnant women. Longitudinal monitoring of weight changes, metabolic comorbidities, and other clinical risk factors is also recommended to optimize patient management and retention. Early warning indicators (EWIs) of HIV drug resistance assess the quality of ART programs and identify gaps in service delivery. Monitoring EWIs helps minimize the emergence of drug resistance and optimize program performance. WHO recommends annual EWI monitoring to track improvements or declines over time and identify clinics needing additional support. Addressing gaps in adherence, drug stock-outs, and timely regimen switches can reduce the risk of resistance and virological failure. In summary, strengthening patient monitoring systems, addressing gaps in care, and implementing WHO-recommended guidelines are critical for improving HIV treatment outcomes, reducing mortality, and achieving global targets for HIV care.
